\chapter{Design Analysis}

The design analysis of the electromagnetic brake joint is divided into four hierarchical layers, including the WSoI which encompasses the testing enviornment and the PCMA arm, the NSoI representing the joint, its functional subsystems, and the individual components. The physical development of the joint was iterative, however, the resulting architecture is documented in a logical, top-down fashion instead of a chronological sequence. To describe the system's integration, the analysis is split into three domains which constitute the mechanical design, the electronic design, and the software design. The mechanical design outlines the physical configuration and loading paths. The electronic design describes the peripheral circuitry and power interfacing. The software design defines the control logic and the state machine controlling the electromagnetic brake.

\section{Mechanical Design}

Figure~\ref{fig:screenshot-2026-10-21-103108} shows the 3D CAD assembly of the electromagnetic brake joint produced as part of the detailed design analysis following the integration and refinement of the subsystem concepts.
\begin{figure}[H]
	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{"../../../../../../../../../Downloads/Screenshot 2026-10-21 103108"}
	\caption{Electromagnetic Brake Assembly}
	\label{fig:screenshot-2026-10-21-103108}
\end{figure}
The top-level system elements are listed in the drawing's parts list and are marked with balloon item numbers in Figure~\ref{fig:screenshot-2026-10-21-103108}.The engineering drawings in Appendix~\ref{app:drawing_pack} detail the physical mounting interfaces with external structural components, as well as the spatial clearance limits defined for the joint mechanism within the NSoI.

Material selection for the joint assembly is governed by two competing engineering requirements, which include minimizing moving inertia and maximizing magnetic performance:
\begin{itemize}
	\item An aluminium alloy, readily available in the workshop,  was chosen for the structural housing, joint shaft, bearing blocks, base link, and articulating link. With an assumed density of $\rho_{\text{Al}} = \SI{2700}{kg/m^3}$, aluminium provides a high strength-to-weight ratio that reduces the overall weight of the extended joint parts and minimises the twisting force caused by its own gravity. This enables precise manual arm manipulation without excessive user fatigue.
	\item A mild steel alloy, also readily availble in the workshop, was chosen specifically for the electromagnet yoke, solenoid cores, pressure tabs, and friction plate. Ferromagnetic mild steel exhibits high magnetic permeability ($\mu_r \approx 2000$) and a high saturation flux density ($B_{\text{sat}} \approx \SI{1.6}{T}$). This allows the magnetic field lines to flow easily and densely through the steel component. It is also important to notes that, its low coercive force minimizes residual magnetism ($B_r$) upon power cutoff, which ensures immediate mechanical disengagement when the brake is de-energized.
	\item A hardwood disc with an assumed $\mu = 0.6$ mating against mild steel, provides a high coefficient of static friction without cold-welding, while a brass key transmits torque to the shaft without inducing magnetic leakage.
\end{itemize}

The overall configuration uses the designed electromagnetic brake assemblymounted coaxially on the joint shaft with the rest of the joint components. The joint shaft is supported by two RS PRO \SI{20}{mm} ID double-row ball bearings mounted with an interference fit and secured with RS PRO \SI{32}{mm} OD one-piece steel shaft collars to prevent axial slipping. The bearing housing are integrated directly into the stationary joint housing. The joint housing clamps down onto the electromagnetic cover and holds the rotary encoder body stationary. The rotary encoder, a GTS06-OC-RA1000B-2M optical encoder (\SI{1000}{PPR}) is fitted into a centered axial borehole and clamped via a grub screw onto the encoder shaft flat. This allows the encoder shaft to rotate with the joint shaft, to measure relative angular displacement (refer to Drawing 24989142-01-00-00 in Appendix~\ref{app:drawing_pack}). On the opposite end, the electromagnetic brake assembly directly interfaces with the shaft. The assembly consists of the four solenoid yokes, four solenoid coils, a welded, mild-steel cover, laser-cut mild steel friction plate (laser-cut by Fabrinox), and wooden brake disc.

The mechanical load path originates at the articulating link assembly ($m_{\text{link}} = \SI{0.4659}{kg}$, including the link pipe, probe hub, and measuring probe). Gravity acting on this mass at an effective moment arm of $l_{\text{link}} = \SI{0.325}{m}$ generates a static gravitational torque. Accounting for a safety factor of $1.5$, the actual verified link holding torque is calculated as $T_{\text{holding, verified}} = \SI{2.228}{N.m}$ (Equation~\ref{eq:Articulation_link_weight_app} in Appendix~\ref{sec:link_mass_calc}). Because this holding torque is within bounds of the TPM\_03, calculations following the determination of $T_{\text{holding}}$ will use the initially set \SI{7.725}{Nm}. The torque is countered across the friction interface between the rotating wooden disc and the non-rotating mild steel friction plate. Operating under assumed uniform pressure with a friction coefficient of $\mu = 0.35$, the required axial clamping force generated across this interface is $F_{\text{clamping}} = \SI{636.88}{N}$ (Equation~\ref{eq:F_holding_app} in Appendix~\ref{sec:brake_sizing_calc}). When power is cut off, the mild steel pressure tabs deliver a combined electromagnetic clamping force of \SI{3550}{N} (well exceeding the \SI{383.18}{N} threshold), pushing the friction plate flush against the brake disc.

This coaxial configuration helps maintain a uniform clamping force distribution that minimizes parasitic shaft deflections. Additionally, housing the brake internally allows the joint to achieve its required \SI{90}{\degree} operational articulation sweep.

Detailed Free Body Diagrams (FBDs), stress analysis derivations, and full numerical holding force calculations supporting these operational conditions are provided in Appendix~\ref{sec:link_mass_calc}.

\section{Electrical Design}

The purpose of the switching circuit is to safely bridge the power gap between the low-power control and data management logic and the high-power electromagnetic brake. The STM32 Nucleo microcontroller operates on a $3.3\text{ V}$ logic level with general purpose input/output (GPIO) pins that supply a maximum current of $25\text{ mA}$. In contrast, the full-scale electromagnetic joint brake requires an operating current of $I_{\text{total}} = 8\text{ A}$ at $V_{\text{DC}} = 24\text{ V}$. A direct connection between these two components would cause catastrophic failure of the microcontroller. As a result, a dedicated power-stepping, gate-driving, and switching circuit is required to isolate the logic hardware, protect against inductive transients caused by the electromagnet's actuation, and efficiently switch the high-current coil load. 

Figure~\ref{fig:wiring-diagram} details the physical architecture of the electrical subsystem.
\begin{figure}[h]
	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{"../../../../../../../../../Downloads/Wiring Diagram (5)"}
	\caption{Wiring and Interconnect Diagram for the Full-Scale Joint Mechanism}
	\label{fig:wiring-diagram}
\end{figure}
To generate the required total clamping force, four identical solenoids are utilised within the electromagnet. Choosing between a parallel or series electrical interconnection significantly impacts circuit reliability, supply voltage requirements, and coil winding specifications:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Supply Voltage and Current Distribution: In a series connection, the $24\text{ V}$ supply voltage is divided equally across the four coils ($6\text{ V}$ per coil), while the full line current of $8\text{ A}$ flows sequentially through every solenoid. Achieving $8\text{ A}$ at $6\text{ V}$ requires an extremely low coil resistance ($R_{\text{coil}} = 0.75\,\Omega$), demanding thick gauge wire that is difficult to wind densely. As opposed to a parallel configuration, which delivers the full $24\text{ V}_{\text{DC}}$ across each solenoid. The $8\text{ A}$ total supply current divides equally among the four parallel branches ($I_{\text{sol}} = 2\text{ A}$ per coil), resulting in a manageable coil resistance requirement of $R_{\text{coil}} = 12\,\Omega$.
	\item Redundancy and fault-finding: In a series configuration, an open-circuit failure in a single solenoid winding disrupts the current path for the entire brake system, leading to complete joint failure. In a parallel configuration, each solenoid operates independently. If one coil open-circuits, the remaining three solenoids continue to generate holding force.
	\item Inductive Time Constant ($\tau = L/R$): A parallel connection maintains high single-coil resistance relative to inductance, which minimises current rise delays during actuation and ensures rapid flux buildup.
\end{itemize}
Therefore, the parallel configuration was selected for the full-scale joint assembly.

To supply the low-voltage control and feedback hardware from the primary $24\text{ V}_{\text{DC}}$ DC supply, an XL7015 step-down buck converter is integrated into the power rail. The XL7015 accepts an input voltage range of $0\text{--}80\text{ V}_{\text{DC}}$ and steps it down to a regulated $5\text{ V}$ output voltage that is suitable for powering the STM32 microcontroller board and the GTS06-OC-RA1000B optical rotary encoder. A high-efficiency DC-DC buck converter ($\eta \approx 85\text{--}90\%$) ensures stable voltage delivery during high-current load switching transients.

To control the energization of the $24\text{ V} / 8\text{ A}$ electromagnetic coil array, an N-channel Power MOSFET is utilized in a low-side switching topology acting as a solid-state digital relay. 

To control the actuation of the electromagnet, an N-channel Power MOSFET (Infineon IRF640N) is deployed in a high-side of the switching circuit acting as a solid-state digital relay.

Because the IRF640N requires a gate-to-source voltage ($V_{GS}$) of at least $10\text{ V}$ to achieve full channel enhancement and minimum on-state resistance, driving its gate directly from the STM32's native $3.3\text{ V}$ logic signal would operate the MOSFET in its linear region. This would cause excessive thermal runaway and catastrophic damage. To bridge this voltage threshold using components available in the laboratories under the Electrical and Electronics Department, a discrete 2N3904 NPN BJT level-shifter stage is integrated as a gate pre-driver.

The STM32 GPIO signal drives the base of the 2N3904 through a current-limiting resistor of \SI{1}{k\ohm}. When turned off, the 2N3904's collector is pulled up to a $12\text{ V}$ supply rail via a pull-up resistor ($R_{PU} = 2.2\text{ k}\Omega$), delivering $V_{GS} \approx 9.84\text{ V}$ directly to the IRF640N gate. Driven at to saturation, the IRF640N operates at its rated static drain-to-source resistance $R_{DS(\text{on})} = 0.15\,\Omega$. At the full operating load of $I_{\text{total}} = 8\text{ A}$, the continuous conduction power dissipation $P_{\text{cond}}$ across the MOSFET is:
\begin{equation}
	P_{\text{cond}} = I_{\text{total}}^2 \cdot R_{DS(\text{on})} = (8\text{ A})^2 \cdot 0.15\,\Omega = 9.6\text{ W}
\end{equation}
To dissipate this heat continuously and maintain the junction temperature ($T_J$) safely below $175^\circ\text{C}$, the TO-220 packaged MOSFET is fitted with a dedicated aluminum heatsink ($R_{\text{th,sa}} \le 3.5^\circ\text{C/W}$).

To maintain the circuit's operability, protect the microcontroller, and ensure reliable gate-driving levels, specific passive components are incorporated as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:wiring-diagram}:
\begin{itemize}
	\item A base-limiting resistor of \SI{1}{k\ohm} is placed between the STM32 GPIO signal pin and the base of the 2N3904 NPN transistor. Sizing this resistor restricts the continuous base current drawn from the microcontroller GPIO pin during active switching to as seen under Equation~\ref{eq:ajkva}:
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:ajkva}
		I_B = \frac{V_{\text{GPIO}} - V_{BE}}{R_B} = \frac{3.3\text{ V} - 0.7\text{ V}}{1000\,\Omega} = 2.6\text{ mA}
	\end{equation}
	which safely complies with the STM32 absolute maximum output pin threshold of $25\text{ mA}$.
	
	\item A collector pull-Up resistor of $\SI{2.2}{k\ohm}$ is connected between the $24\text{ V}$ DC power supply and the 2N3904 collector node (which connects directly to the IRF640N MOSFET Gate). When the 2N3904 is turned off (GPIO LOW), this resistor pulls the MOSFET Gate voltage up toward the rail, which provides sufficient gate-to-source voltage ($V_{GS}$) to fully enhance the IRF640N power MOSFET into saturation.
	
	\item A gate pull-down resistor of $\SI{10}{k\ohm}$ is connected between the IRF640N MOSFET Gate and Ground (GND). In conjunction with collector pull-down resistor, it forms a voltage divider establishing an active gate drive voltage when the 2N3904 is off, as shown under Equation~\ref{eq:kvlbs}:
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:kvlbs}
		V_{GS} = V_{\text{rail}} \cdot \left( \frac{R_{PD}}{R_{PU} + R_{PD}} \right) = 24\text{ V} \cdot \left( \frac{10\text{ k}\Omega}{2.2\text{ k}\Omega + 10\text{ k}\Omega} \right) \approx 19.67\text{ V}
	\end{equation}
	This maximizes channel conductivity while remaining safely within the IRF640N maximum absolute gate rating ($V_{GS(\text{max})} = \pm 20\text{ V}$). Additionally, during microcontroller boot or floating GPIO states, $R_{PD}$ keeps the gate referenced to Ground.
	
	\item An flyback diode is placed in parallel across the electromagnetic coil array terminals. When the MOSFET switches off to disengage the joint, the collapsing magnetic field in the coil induction induces a severe negative Back-Electromotive Force (Back-EMF) spike ($v_L = -L \frac{di}{dt}$). The flyback diode array provides a means of dissipating the $8\text{ A}$ inductive current without exceeding the MOSFET breakdown rating ($V_{(BR)DSS} = 200\text{ V}$).
\end{itemize}

For real-time spatial positioning and angular displacement tracking, the GTS06-OC-RA1000B optical rotary encoder ($1000\text{ PPR}$) is connected across the $5\text{ V}$ regulated by the DC-DC buck converter. Its A and B quadrature signal lines are routed directly to the STM32 timer input pins configured in encoder interface mode. 

Complete thermal dissipation modeling, component voltage/current distributions, and solenoid winding derivations based on the required holding clamping force are presented in Appendix~\ref{app:design_calc}.

\section{Software Design}

In mechatronics systems, such as the electromagnetic brake system, it is necessary to define the interactions between actuators (electrmoangetic brake), sensors (encoder), and the control software for reliable operation. The software architecture for the brake system uses a supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) hierachy to manage real-time monitoring and actuation processes. This hierarchy consists of the following levels, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:softwareflowchart}:

\begin{itemize}
	\item Level 0 (field devices) consists of the hardware interacting directly with the optical rotary encoder, the IRF640N MOSFET, and the electromagnet brake.
	\item Level 1 (control logic) is executed by the STM32 Nucleo microcontroller, which acts as input/output processing module.
	\item Level 2 (supervisory) is handled by the connected computer that recieves angular displacement data from the microcontroller for logging and visualisation.
\end{itemize}

To fulfill the system's FRs, the microcontroller's pinout is configured to interface with the Level 0 devices. The rotary encoder's Phase A and Phase B signal lines are connected to pins PA0 and PA1. These pins are routed internally to the STM32's hardware timer (TIM2). The encoder outputs a quadrature pulse\footnote{A quadrature pulse is a signal that consists of two identical square waves offset by \SI{90}{\degree}.}, which allows the system to determine rotational position and direction of the shaft based on which phase leads the other. By utilising X4 encoding, which is when pulses are counting on the rising and falling edge, for both channels, the 1000 pulse per revolution (PPR) encoder yields 4000 distinct counts per 360-degree rotation.

By operating TIM2 in Encoder Mode, the microcontroller is able to use its dedicated hardware circuitry to autonomously track the high-frequency quadrature pulses and update a 32-bit memory register entirely in the background. This type of tracking eliminates the need for CPU-intensive interrupts, which would force the processor to halt execution of the code to count thousands of pulses per second. As a result, the CPU is freed up to properly manage other tasks. Additionally, the MOSFET gate is driven by pin PC2, which is configured as a digital output. Pin PC13 is configured as a hardware interrupt (EXTI), which is tied to the user input button. Lastly, pins PA2 and PA3 are configured for USART2 serial transmission to communicate the level 2  supervisory computer.

The control strategy implemented for the electromagnetic brake is an open-loop, bang-bang controller. Due to the binary mechanical requirement\footnote{The joint must be locked in placed, or released, free to rotate.}, duty cycle control is unnecessary. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:softwareflowchart}, the system initialises into a locked state by defaulting PC2 low, thereby creating a fail-safe protocol. 

\begin{figure}[H]
	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=0.52\linewidth]{../../../../../../../../../Downloads/Software_Flowchart}
	\caption{Software Design of the PCMA Operation}
	\label{fig:softwareflowchart}
\end{figure}

The main loop reads the 32-bit counter from TIM2, converts the raw pulse count into an angular displacement into degrees, and transmits this data at \SI{20}{Hz} to the supervisor computer via USART2.

To manage the energisation and de-energisation of the electromagnet, the software uses the external interrupt on PC13. When the user presses the button, the interrupt service routine (ISR) pauses the main looop and toggles the joint's variable (joint\_locked) state. If the variable goes high (joint\_locked == 1), the controller drives the MOSFET gate high (\SI{3.3}{V}). This energises the solenoid and opens the air gap. Due to the asynchronous execution of the interrupt, the user does not experience lag when manually operating the arm. This is done to ensure a seamless human machine interface (HMI) between the mechanical operation and the software control state.
